questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: They arrived ___ the airport just before boarding began.
questions.e: 'Arrive at' for specific places; 'arrive in' for cities/countries.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: She has been interested ___ astronomy since childhood.
questions.e: Fixed collocation: 'interested in'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The professor objected ___ the proposal on ethical grounds.
questions.e: Fixed collocation: 'object to'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Divide the grant money ___ the three research teams.
questions.e: 'Between' is standard for distinct individual recipients, even when more than two.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The workshop aims to inform, to educate, and ___ the participants.
questions.e: Parallel infinitives: 'to inform, to educate, and to inspire'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: She enjoys reading novels, watching documentaries, and ___ essays.
questions.e: Parallel gerunds: 'reading..., watching..., and writing...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The new policy is neither fair nor ___.
questions.e: 'Neither/nor' must join identical structures: 'neither fair nor practical'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: He is known for his honesty, his dedication, and ___.
questions.e: Parallel noun phrases: 'his honesty, his dedication, and his hard work'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The committee decided to postpone the event, revise the budget, and ___ new members.
questions.e: Parallel base verbs after 'decided to': 'postpone..., revise..., and recruit...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Good notes should be concise, accurate, and ___.
questions.e: Parallel adjectives: 'concise, accurate, and legible'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: She not only won the debate but also ___ the essay competition.
questions.e: 'Not only...but also' joins parallel verbs: 'not only won... but also won...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The course covers grammar, vocabulary, and ___ skills.
questions.e: Parallel nouns: 'grammar, vocabulary, and writing skills'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: To succeed, one must study regularly, practise deliberately, and ___.
questions.e: Parallel base verbs: 'study..., practise..., and seek...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The report was thorough, well-organised, and ___.
questions.e: Parallel adjectives: 'thorough, well-organised, and convincing'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Either you submit the form today or ___ it tomorrow.
questions.e: 'Either...or' joins parallel verb phrases: 'submit... or collect...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Her duties include answering queries, maintaining records, and ___ reports.
questions.e: Parallel gerunds after 'include': 'answering..., maintaining..., and preparing...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If it rains tomorrow, the outdoor ceremony ___.
questions.e: Type 1 (real future): 'If it rains, ... will be cancelled'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If I had more time, I ___ volunteer at the library.
questions.e: Type 2 (unreal present): 'If I had..., I would...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If she had revised thoroughly, she ___ the examination.
questions.e: Type 3 (unreal past): 'If she had revised, she would have passed'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If he had taken the earlier train, he ___ here by now.
questions.e: Mixed conditional: past condition, present result — 'would be here by now'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Unless the funding arrives soon, the project ___.
questions.e: 'Unless' + present, future result: 'will have to stop'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If you heat ice, it ___.
questions.e: Zero conditional for general truths: present simple in both clauses.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Had the alarm worked, the residents ___ evacuated in time.
questions.e: Inverted Type 3: 'Had the alarm worked, ... would have been evacuated'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If I were the dean, I ___ the library hours extended.
questions.e: Type 2 with subjunctive 'were': 'I would get the hours extended'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Should you need any assistance, ___ the help desk.
questions.e: 'Should you need' (formal Type 1 inversion) takes the imperative: 'contact the help desk'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If they ___ the deadline, they would have received the grant.
questions.e: Type 3 requires past perfect in the if-clause: 'had met'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: I would lend you my notes if I ___ them with me.
questions.e: Type 2: 'if I had them with me' (unreal present).

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: If the data ___ accurate, the conclusions must be revised.
questions.e: Type 1 real condition about the present: 'If the data is not accurate...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The samples ___ in the laboratory yesterday afternoon.
questions.e: Simple past passive for a finished past event: 'were analysed'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The new metro line ___ by the end of next year.
questions.e: Future perfect passive for completion by a future point: 'will have been completed'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The manuscript ___ to three publishers before it was accepted.
questions.e: Past perfect passive for the earlier past event: 'had been sent'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Participants ___ to switch off their phones during the session.
questions.e: Passive needed: participants receive the request — 'were asked'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The bridge ___ for repairs every five years.
questions.e: Present simple passive for routine actions: 'is inspected'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The error ___ before the report was submitted.
questions.e: Past perfect passive: the correction preceded the submission.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: All applications must ___ by 31 March.
questions.e: Modal + passive infinitive: 'must be submitted'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The old building ___ down to make way for the library.
questions.e: Passive: the building receives the action — 'was pulled down'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: She ___ the award for her contribution to research.
questions.e: 'Was presented with the award' — the preposition 'with' is required.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The results ___ in a peer-reviewed journal last month.
questions.e: Simple past passive for a dated past event: 'were published'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The professor ___ lecture we attended yesterday is world-renowned.
questions.e: 'Whose' shows possession: 'whose lecture we attended'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: This is the laboratory ___ the breakthrough experiment was conducted.
questions.e: Formal: 'in which the experiment was conducted' (or 'where'). 'In which' is the most precise formal choice.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The committee approved the proposal, ___ surprised everyone.
questions.e: Non-defining clause referring to the whole previous clause: ', which surprised everyone'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Anyone ___ wishes to participate should register online.
questions.e: 'Who' as subject of 'wishes': 'Anyone who wishes...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The reason ___ she resigned was never made public.
questions.e: 'The reason why...' is the standard collocation (or 'the reason that').

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: He cited several studies, most of ___ were published after 2020.
questions.e: After a preposition in a non-defining clause, use 'which': 'most of which'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The student ___ you met at the conference won the scholarship.
questions.e: Formal object form after a preposition-less verb: 'whom you met' (also acceptable: 'who/that').

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Delhi, ___ the conference will be held, is well connected by metro.
questions.e: Non-defining clause for a place: ', where the conference will be held,' (or 'in which').

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The method ___ the researchers used proved highly effective.
questions.e: Defining object clause: 'that the researchers used' ('which' also works; 'whom/whose' do not).

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: My supervisor, ___ guidance was invaluable, retired last month.
questions.e: Possessive relative: 'whose guidance'. 'That' cannot follow a comma.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: ___ the document carefully, the lawyer signed it.
questions.e: Perfect participle for the earlier action with the correct subject: 'Having reviewed..., the lawyer signed'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Walking to the laboratory, ___.
o: the samples were dropped by me
questions.e: The participle's subject must be the main subject: 'Walking..., I dropped the samples'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: She bought a ___ vase at the auction.
questions.e: Adjective order: opinion → age → origin: 'beautiful old Chinese vase'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: ___ in 2010, the policy has shaped education ever since.
questions.e: Past participle phrase with passive meaning: 'Introduced in 2010, the policy has...'

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The researchers found the results ___.
questions.e: '-ing' adjectives describe things: 'surprising results'; '-ed' describes feelings.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: ___ the instructions, the technician calibrated the device.
questions.e: Present participle for a simultaneous/just-prior action by the subject: 'Following the instructions...'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: He spoke in a voice ___ audible at the back of the hall.
questions.e: Adverb needed to modify 'audible': 'barely audible'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Exhausted after the marathon, ___.
questions.e: Dangling modifier fixed: the subject 'he' matches 'exhausted'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The committee will review the proposal ___ submitted last week.
questions.e: Reduced relative clause needs the full form here for clarity: 'that was submitted' ('submitted last week' alone is also grammatical, but among the options only 'that was' completes the clause correctly).

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Only ___ the invitation did she learn about the venue change.
questions.e: 'Only after receiving...' — gerund after the preposition; 'after received' is ungrammatical.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The results were ___ significant to justify further funding.
questions.e: Adverb modifies the adjective 'significant': 'sufficiently significant'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: There has been a ___ improvement in air quality this year.
questions.e: Adjective modifies the noun 'improvement': 'a noticeable improvement'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The discovery ___ our understanding of the disease.
questions.e: Verb needed as predicate: 'revolutionised our understanding'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The committee reached a ___ decision after hours of debate.
questions.e: Adjective modifies 'decision': 'a unanimous decision'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: She presented her findings ___ and confidently.
questions.e: Adverb modifies the verb 'presented': 'presented her findings clearly'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The ___ of the new policy surprised even its supporters.
questions.e: Noun needed as subject: 'The rapidity of the new policy...'

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: His argument was both logical and ___.
questions.e: Parallel adjectives after 'both': 'logical and persuasive'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The equipment must be handled with ___.
questions.e: Noun after 'with': 'with caution'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The lecture was ___ long, but the content was excellent.
questions.e: Adverb modifies the adjective 'long': 'excessively long'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: A ___ analysis of the data revealed two distinct patterns.
questions.e: Adjective modifies 'analysis': 'A careful analysis'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The new regulations will ___ affect small businesses.
questions.e: Adverb modifies the verb 'affect': 'will adversely affect'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Her ___ to detail impressed the entire panel.
questions.e: Noun needed: 'Her attention to detail' (fixed collocation).

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The climate of Bengaluru is milder than ___ of Delhi.
questions.e: 'That of Delhi' = 'the climate of Delhi' — singular 'that' for singular 'climate'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: This year's intake is ___ than last year's.
questions.e: One-syllable adjectives take '-er': 'larger'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Of the three proposals, this one is ___.
questions.e: Superlative with 'the' for three or more: 'the most practical'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The new model is twice ___ the previous one.
questions.e: 'Twice as + adjective + as' for multiples: 'twice as efficient as'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: She speaks English ___ fluently as her colleagues.
questions.e: 'As fluently as' — the 'as...as' structure for equality.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The more you practise, ___.
questions.e: Double comparative: 'The more..., the more confident you become'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: His second novel is far ___ interesting than his first.
questions.e: 'Far more interesting than' — 'far' intensifies the comparative.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: This is one of the ___ discoveries of the decade.
questions.e: 'One of the most significant' — superlative after 'one of the'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The task turned out to be ___ difficult than expected.
questions.e: Comparative with 'than expected': 'more difficult than expected'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Iron is ___ useful metal in construction.
questions.e: 'The most useful' — superlative with 'the'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Their new campus is not ___ large as the old one.
questions.e: Negative equality: 'not as large as'.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The findings were ___ surprising, given the small sample.
questions.e: 'Hardly surprising' = barely surprising — the intended meaning with the small sample.

In the sentence below, the word lucid is closest in meaning to ___.

In the sentence below, the word precipitous is closest in meaning to ___.

questions.e: 'Precipitous' means dangerously steep/sudden.

questions.q:

questions.e: 'Incompatible' means unable to exist together — 'unable to coexist'.

questions.q:

questions.e: 'Acrimonious' means bitter in tone.

The Science of Sleep and Memory
Sleep is not a passive shutdown of the brain but an active process essential for learning. During deep sleep, the brain replays patterns of neural activity first observed during waking hours, effectively rehearsing new information. This replay occurs primarily in the hippocampus, a structure critical for forming new memories, which then transfers stabilised information to the cortex for long-term storage.
Research demonstrates that students who sleep after studying recall significantly more than those who remain awake for an equivalent period. Even short naps of 60 to 90 minutes can improve retention, provided they include deep-sleep phases. Conversely, sleep deprivation impairs the prefrontal cortex, reducing attention, judgement and the ability to form new memories the following day.
The implications for education are considerable. Cramming through the night — a common student strategy — is among the least effective ways to learn, because it deprives the brain of the very process that consolidates knowledge. Spaced study sessions separated by sleep consistently outperform marathon sessions, a finding now supported by decades of controlled experiments.

What is the main idea of the passage?
o: The hippocampus stores all memories permanently
Sleep actively consolidates learning and memory
questions.e: The passage argues sleep is an active process that consolidates learning.

Urban Green Spaces
As cities expand, urban planners increasingly recognise parks and green corridors not as decorative luxuries but as essential infrastructure. Vegetation cools surrounding air through shade and evapotranspiration, measurably reducing the urban heat-island effect: neighbourhoods near large parks can be 2–3°C cooler than built-up districts nearby.
Beyond temperature, green spaces deliver documented public-health benefits. Residents living within walking distance of a park report lower stress levels and higher rates of physical activity. Economically, well-maintained parks raise adjacent property values and attract tourism, often returning far more than their upkeep costs. Critics argue that land in growing cities is too valuable to 'waste' on parks, yet cost-benefit analyses repeatedly show green infrastructure paying for itself through health savings, energy reduction and increased commerce.
The challenge is equitable distribution. Affluent districts typically enjoy abundant greenery while low-income neighbourhoods — which would benefit most — have the least. Progressive cities now mandate minimum green-space standards for new developments, treating access to nature as a matter of public equity rather than privilege.

questions.q:
The Rise of Antibiotic Resistance
Antibiotics rank among the greatest medical advances in history, yet their effectiveness is eroding. Bacteria evolve rapidly, and each use of an antibiotic creates selective pressure: susceptible bacteria die while resistant mutants survive and multiply. Over decades of overuse — in human medicine and, massively, in livestock farming — resistant strains have proliferated worldwide.
The consequences are stark. Infections once cured in days, such as certain urinary-tract and wound infections, now require last-resort drugs or fail to respond at all. The World Health Organization identifies antimicrobial resistance among the top ten global public-health threats, estimating millions of deaths annually linked to drug-resistant infections.
Solutions exist but demand coordination. Doctors must prescribe antibiotics only when necessary and complete appropriate courses; patients must not demand them for viral illnesses like colds, against which they are useless. In agriculture, several countries have banned growth-promoting antibiotics, slowing resistance without harming productivity.
Perhaps most crucial is the development pipeline: few new antibiotic classes have reached the market in thirty years because they are less profitable than chronic-disease drugs. Public funding and new incentive models are now attempting to revive research. Without such efforts, medicine risks sliding back toward an era when a simple scratch could kill.

o: Antibiotic resistance is a growing global threat requiring coordinated action
questions.e: The passage describes the threat and the coordinated solutions needed.

The Economics of Renewable Energy
A decade ago, renewable energy required heavy subsidies to compete with fossil fuels. That equation has inverted: in most markets, new solar and wind installations now produce electricity more cheaply than new coal or gas plants. The driver is the learning curve — every doubling of installed solar capacity has historically cut costs by roughly 20%, a pattern that has held for forty years.
The transition, however, faces a structural challenge: intermittency. Solar panels produce nothing at night, and wind turbines stand idle in calm weather. Solving this requires a portfolio approach — geographically dispersed generation, strengthened transmission grids, demand that shifts to match supply, and storage. Battery costs have fallen nearly 90% since 2010, making short-term storage economical, though seasonal storage remains unsolved.
Critics point to the mineral intensity of clean technologies: an electric car needs far more copper, lithium and rare earths than a conventional one. Yet lifecycle analyses consistently find that, even accounting for mining and manufacturing, renewables and electric vehicles produce a fraction of the emissions of fossil alternatives over their lifetimes.
The economic question has therefore shifted from whether clean energy can compete to how fast infrastructure, markets and policy can absorb it. Countries that invested early now dominate supply chains — a reminder that energy transitions are industrial competitions as much as environmental ones.

How Forests Communicate
Beneath a forest floor lies an unseen network: fine fungal threads called mycelium connect the roots of different trees, forming what scientists term a mycorrhizal network. Through these threads, trees exchange nutrients — a shaded seedling may receive carbon from a sunlit adult — and even transmit warning signals about insect attacks, prompting neighbours to produce defensive chemicals.
This discovery has reshaped how biologists view forests: not as collections of competing individuals but as cooperative systems, at least in part. The largest, oldest trees — sometimes called 'mother trees' — act as hubs, supporting dozens of younger trees through the network. Experiments using labelled carbon have traced its movement from tree to tree, confirming the transfers are real and substantial.
Sceptics urge caution. They note that fungi are not altruistic messengers but traders: they take a significant share of the carbon for themselves, and some observed transfers might reflect fungal self-interest rather than tree cooperation. The network metaphor, they argue, risks overstating intentionality in what may be largely chemical exchange.
Nevertheless, the findings have practical consequences. Clear-cutting that removes hub trees can collapse the network, leaving replanted seedlings to struggle. Foresters increasingly retain veteran trees during harvesting — a small change in practice rooted in a profound shift in understanding.

o: Forests are linked by fungal networks that exchange resources, reshaping our view of them

questions.q:
How Forests Communicate
Beneath a forest floor lies an unseen network: fine fungal threads called mycelium connect the roots of different trees, forming what scientists term a mycorrhizal network. Through these threads, trees exchange nutrients — a shaded seedling may receive carbon from a sunlit adult — and even transmit warning signals about insect attacks, prompting neighbours to produce defensive chemicals.
This discovery has reshaped how biologists view forests: not as collections of competing individuals but as cooperative systems, at least in part. The largest, oldest trees — sometimes called 'mother trees' — act as hubs, supporting dozens of younger trees through the network. Experiments using labelled carbon have traced its movement from tree to tree, confirming the transfers are real and substantial.
Sceptics urge caution. They note that fungi are not altruistic messengers but traders: they take a significant share of the carbon for themselves, and some observed transfers might reflect fungal self-interest rather than tree cooperation. The network metaphor, they argue, risks overstating intentionality in what may be largely chemical exchange.
Nevertheless, the findings have practical consequences. Clear-cutting that removes hub trees can collapse the network, leaving replanted seedlings to struggle. Foresters increasingly retain veteran trees during harvesting — a small change in practice rooted in a profound shift in understanding.

questions.e: 'Clear-cutting that removes hub trees can collapse the network.'

Tidal Power
Of all renewable energy sources, tides are the most predictable — and engineers are learning to harness them. Unlike wind or sunlight, tidal flows follow lunar cycles that can be forecast years in advance, making grid integration far simpler.
The engineering challenge is the marine environment itself. Salt water corrodes machinery, and turbines must survive powerful currents while avoiding harm to fish and marine mammals. Because installation costs are high, tidal projects need decades to become competitive with wind and solar.
Advocates argue the reliability justifies the expense. A tidal lagoon can generate electricity for over a century with minimal fuel costs, and predictable output reduces the need for expensive battery storage.

The word harness in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to ___.
questions.e: 'Harness' = put something to use (here, making the tides generate power).

Student: Hi — I have an essay draft due Friday, and I am not sure my argument is clear. Do I need an appointment to get feedback?
Advisor: For a full draft review, yes — appointments are 45 minutes. But we also do 15-minute walk-in sessions for quick questions.
Student: My draft is pretty rough. I will take the full session, then.
Advisor: Good call. Book online — the slots before Friday fill up fast.

Why does the student decide to book an appointment?
o: She wants a full review of her rough draft
She needs to complain about a grade

Thawing Permafrost
Beneath much of the Arctic lies permafrost — ground that has stayed frozen for thousands of years. As temperatures rise, this layer is thawing, releasing methane that was locked in ancient organic matter. Because methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide in the short term, scientists worry the thaw could accelerate warming further.
The thaw also undermines infrastructure. Roads, pipelines and buildings across Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada were built on the assumption that the ground would stay frozen; as it softens, maintenance costs are climbing sharply.

What can be inferred from the passage about infrastructure in the far north?
o: It was designed for conditions that no longer hold
It is now cheaper to maintain
It caused the permafrost to thaw
It is unaffected by methane release
questions.e: The passage states infrastructure was built assuming permanently frozen ground — an assumption the thaw is now invalidating.

According to the passage, what is the immediate effect of the injunction for current F-1 students?
o: They continue to be admitted for the duration of their programmes
They must complete their studies within four years
Their OPT work authorisation is cancelled
The 60-day grace period is reduced to 30 days
questions.e: The passage states the injunction preserves the existing system: admission for the duration of the programme, the 60-day grace period and OPT. The other options describe the blocked rule, which is not in effect.

August 2026 recorded the busiest month ever for study visas
Main-applicant applications grew 16% year on year

Indian students stopped applying to US colleges entirely
The visa crackdown affected only students from India

Australia has announced changes to several temporary visa categories as part of measures to reduce net overseas migration, targeting 245,000 arrivals in 2026–27. International students seeking another Student visa from within Australia will generally be expected to progress to a higher-level qualification. The government also plans a ballot for second- and third-year Working Holiday visas, with up to 45,000 second-year and 5,000 third-year visas available annually, and processing times stabilising at around three months.

According to the passage, which of the following is true of the Working Holiday Maker programme?
o: Second-year visas will be granted automatically after regional work
A ballot will allocate up to 45,000 second-year and 5,000 third-year visas a year
The programme is being abolished entirely
All applicants will now wait more than six months
questions.e: The passage states the ballot plan and the 45,000 / 5,000 annual caps explicitly; it contradicts automatic grants, abolition and the six-month claim.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: Australia _____ new visa rules for foreign students on 28 September 2026.
questions.e: A finished event pinned to a specific past date needs the simple past: announced. A fixed past-time marker rules out the present perfect here.

questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.q: (29 Sep 2026) The report says ‘dependants’ of most student visa holders will face new restrictions. A dependant in immigration English is:
o: a university that sponsors the student
a spouse or child attached to a visa holder
an English test the student must pass
questions.e: Dependants are family members — typically spouses or partners and dependent children — attached to the main visa holder. The 17 September announcement restricts exactly this group on most new student and graduate visas.

questions.subject: Reading
questions.q:
Australia’s dependant rule (announced 17 September 2026)
Most international students will not be able to attach family members to new student visas, and the same restriction will apply to graduate visas. Exemptions continue for students from Pacific and ASEAN countries, students undertaking certain courses including PhD programmes, and some government-sponsored students. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government would not separate families already in Australia: ‘Anyone who already has their family attached to a visa and is already here, we’re not going to be breaking up families onshore.’ India is not among the nationality-based exemptions.

What can be inferred about an Indian master’s student already in Australia whose spouse is on their visa?
o: Their spouse’s visa will be cancelled immediately
The government says it will not break up families already onshore
They may now add further dependants after the change
Only ASEAN students are exempt from every restriction
questions.e: Burke’s quoted promise covers families already in Australia; India lacks the nationality exemption, so the second option is the only supported inference. Nothing supports cancellation, new additions or a blanket ASEAN exemption.

questions.subject: Grammar
questions.q: The Working Holiday Maker ballot will offer up to 45,000 second-year visas, _____ is far fewer than many applicants expected.
questions.e: A non-restrictive clause after a comma needs which, referring to the whole preceding offer. That cannot follow a comma in a non-restrictive clause; what and whose do not fit.

capsules.title: TOEFL iBT's January 2026 overhaul: what changed
capsules.body: From 21 January 2026, TOEFL iBT runs under 90 minutes (down from 2 hours) with multistage adaptive Reading and Listening, a new 1–6 band score shown alongside the 0–120 score during a two-year transition, real-life tasks (writing emails, sentence building, a simulated AI interview) and official scores within 72 hours. India fee: about Rs 17,000–18,000.

capsules.subject: Vocabulary
capsules.title: New 1–6 bands: reading your score report
capsules.body: The 1.0–6.0 bands mirror an IELTS-style scale, and universities see both the band and the comparable 0–120 score on your report through the transition. Check each university's stated requirement — some list bands, others the legacy scale — before you apply.

capsules.subject: Grammar
capsules.title: Adaptive sections: why accuracy early matters
capsules.body: In multistage adaptive Reading and Listening, early accuracy unlocks harder second-stage sets — and harder sets unlock higher score ceilings. Bank time for the first section of each adaptive block rather than rushing it.

capsules.subject: Reading
capsules.title: Registration windows: the 7-day rule
capsules.body: TOEFL is offered year-round with 170+ test-centre dates; regular registration closes 7 days before the test and rescheduling closes 4 days before. Book early in peak admission season and keep a buffer for a possible retake.

capsules.subject: General
capsules.title: New TOEFL (1-6 scale) not accepted for Australian visas (Oct 2026)
capsules.body: In January 2026 ETS launched a new version of the TOEFL, with scores from 1 to 6 instead of 0 to 120; universities and many licensing boards already use the new scores. However, as of October 2026 Australia's Department of Home Affairs has not added the new TOEFL to its accepted list. ETS therefore offers a separate product for Australia — 'TOEFL iBT Australia' — which keeps the old format and 0-120 scores and is the TOEFL that counts for Australian visas. Candidates should check the test name says 'TOEFL iBT Australia' when booking, since a new-format score will not count for the visa.

capsules.subject: General
capsules.title: Australia: only test-centre English tests count for visas
capsules.body: Home Affairs overhauled the approved English test list and score tables from 7 August 2025. Accepted tests for Australian visas include IELTS (with One Skill Retake for eligible visas), PTE Academic, OET, TOEFL iBT Australia, CELPIP General, Cambridge C1 Advanced, LanguageCert and the Michigan English Test — all taken at a secure test centre. At-home or online versions are not accepted for visa purposes, and old score tables copied from pre-2025 guides can mislead because requirements were re-mapped test by test.

capsules.subject: TOEFL Updates
capsules.title: TOEFL 2026 redesign: adaptive Reading & Listening; new practical task types
capsules.body: The TOEFL 2026 redesign (launched January 2026 by ETS) restructured all four sections around practical English. The Reading and Listening sections use adaptive technology — the test adjusts to the candidate's performance as the examination progresses. Contemporary language tasks reflect real academic and everyday communication: writing emails, completing sentence-building tasks and responding to interview-style speaking prompts. Candidates should practise varied question formats rather than relying only on older-version preparation material.

capsules.subject: TOEFL Updates
capsules.title: TOEFL 2026 score reporting: ~3 days; valid 2 years; 0-120 + 1-6 CEFR
capsules.body: Under TOEFL 2026, official iBT scores are generally available in the candidate's ETS account about three days after the test date (email notification when ready). Scores remain valid for two years from the test date. ETS reports both the 0-120 scale and a 1-6 CEFR-aligned scale; TOEFL sets no universal passing score — each institution determines its own minimum. Candidates should verify whether target institutions accept the new 1-6 score format.

capsules.subject: Test Updates
capsules.title: New TOEFL (Jan 2026): 1-6 scoring, adaptive sections
capsules.body: 21 Oct 2026. ETS launched a new TOEFL in January 2026: scores now run 1 to 6 instead of 0-120; Reading and Listening sections are adaptive; new task types include writing emails, sentence-building and interview-style speaking prompts. Scores are generally available in about 3 days and remain valid for 2 years. Verify whether your target institution accepts the new 1-6 format. Exam angle: the biggest TOEFL change in years - expect format questions in counselling and prep tests.

TOEFL aspirants: universities still value the TOEFL, but admissions + visa success now jointly decide outcomes — pair a 100+ TOEFL with meticulous, honest documentation.

capsules.subject: English Learning
capsules.title: Multilingual AI wave: Udai (11 languages), JEET AI Hindi tutor — Oct 2026
capsules.body:
21 Oct 2026: At Aadhaar Samvaad 2026, Daffodil Software's Udai mascot AI conversed in 11 languages; JEET AI launched Hindi-first AI tutoring at ₹1,499/month.

TOEFL listening angle: exposure to varied accents and speeds — lectures, conversations, news reports like these — is the most reliable way to lift listening scores. Shadow one news story daily.

capsules.subject: Current affairs
capsules.title: TOEFL 2026: new format, timing and scoring
capsules.body: The revised TOEFL iBT (2026) runs approximately two hours: Reading 30 min, Listening 29 min, Writing 23 min, Speaking 8 min — with Writing now before Speaking. Reading and Listening are adaptive; tasks reflect real academic and everyday communication (emails, sentence building, interview-style speaking, short exchanges). A new 1–6 score sits alongside the 0–120 scale during transition; scores are valid two years. (Dated: 22 Oct 2026)

capsules.subject: Test updates
capsules.title: TOEFL iBT scoring bands (Jan 2026) and AHPRA 2026 nursing minima (22 Oct 2026)
capsules.body: Since January 2026, the TOEFL iBT reports on a 1–6 band scale, with the familiar 0–120 score available as a comparable reference until January 2028. For Australian nursing registration, AHPRA/NMBA's 2026 standard requires TOEFL iBT 91 overall (Listening 22, Reading 22, Writing 23, Speaking 24) for tests taken on or after 23 April 2026. Australia's Home Affairs does not accept fully online/at-home tests (e.g. TOEFL iBT Home Edition). (22 Oct 2026)

capsules.subject: TOEFL Updates
capsules.title: The 2026 TOEFL: what actually changed
capsules.body: Since January 2026 the TOEFL reports 1–6 scores in half-point increments (overall = average of the four sections, rounded to 0.5), adds multistage adaptive Reading and Listening, and gives a comparable 0–120 score during a two-year transition. Visa alert: Australia accepts only TOEFL iBT Australia, not the new 1–6 format.

alerts.title: Australia-bound? Book “TOEFL iBT Australia”, not the regular test
alerts.body: Australia's Department of Home Affairs does not accept the new 1–6-scale TOEFL iBT scores for visa purposes. If your goal is an Australian visa, book the “TOEFL iBT Australia” edition, which reports on the 0–120 scale. Check the Home Affairs English-language page before paying.
